lines.trans: Can you believe it? She wouldn't even listen.
Whose side are you on? Vika's or your friend's?
But that doesn't change the fact you're a bastard.
Keep at it, Kostya, keep at it.
So if I cheated on you...
Kostyan, it's not what you think.

nominative plural, masculine, used as address

meanings.note: often in parenthetical представляешь? = can you imagine?
Secondary conversational sense ('to introduce, present') (someone or something) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Can you believe it, they forgot it in the oven!

examples.text: Ты даже не представляешь, как я устал.
examples.trans: You can't even imagine how tired I am.

examples.text: Представляешь, в духовке забыли! Юль, выйди.
examples.trans: Can you believe it, they forgot it in the oven! Yul, step out.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('she') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.

examples.text: Паша, я больше не хочу о ней слышать. Понял?
examples.trans: Pasha, I don't want to hear about her again. Understood?

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('even') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or discourse tone in spoken dialogue.

Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'лушать'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to listen', forming an aspectual pair with 'послушать'.
the imperative 'слушай' starts a sentence, like 'look, ...'
Secondary conversational sense ('hello (on the phone)') ('Слушаю' = I'm listening) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Слушай, Самсон, я тут подумал. Твой начальник — такой опытный специалист.
examples.trans: Listen, Samson, I've been thinking. Your boss is such an experienced specialist.

meanings.note: goes right before the word it negates
+ instrumental: стал сентиментальным
Secondary conversational sense ('to start (doing)') (+ infinitive) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Ты слишком сентиментальным стал. А лидер должен быть жёстким.
examples.trans: You've become too sentimental. And a leader has to be tough.

meanings.note: меня = me (genitive/accusative), мне = to me (dative)
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
with a past-tense verb: я бы подумал = I would think
wishes: купили бы = we could have bought

examples.text: Я бы на твоём месте подумал.
examples.trans: If I were you, I'd think about it.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'too'.

examples.text: Мы же здесь выросли. И о людях тоже надо думать.
examples.trans: After all, we grew up here. And you have to think about people too.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'in' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('into, to') (+ accusative (where to)) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'sense', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('what do you mean?') ('В смысле?') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: What do you mean? Where is Mishkin?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('you') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'for' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('behind') (+ instrumental) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
in the instrumental: 'кем ты работаешь?'

examples.trans: Arkady Borisovich, who are your rivals?

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'or', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.
Common masculine noun meaning 'friend' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: This is Vanya, my childhood friend.

examples.text: Это Паша, мой заместитель. Это Ваня, друг моего детства.
examples.trans: This is Pasha, my deputy. This is Vanya, my childhood friend.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'of course'.

examples.text: Конечно, помогу. Кто у вас сейчас начальник?
examples.trans: Of course I'll help. Who's your boss now?

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'but', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо ещё.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need more.
I want to, but I can't.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо сделать ещё больше.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need to do even more.

meanings.note: pointing at a thing or a situation; 'это' + noun = 'this is ...'
points at something: это моё = that's mine
Secondary conversational sense ('is') (linking word: главное — это народ) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: And this is for you. A toy car!

meanings.note: Prefix 'от-' ('away from, off') marks separation, completion, or response (stem 'менять'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'cancels'.

examples.text: Но это не отменяет того, что ты козел.
examples.trans: But that doesn't change the fact you're a bastard.

examples.text: Но это совсем не отменяет твоей сегодняшней смены.
examples.trans: But that does not cancel your shift today at all.

examples.text: Гость позвонил в ресторан и попросил не отменять бронь.
examples.trans: The guest called the restaurant and asked not to cancel the reservation.

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('that') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.
in 'то, что ...' = 'what, the thing that'
High-frequency Russian pronoun ('what') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('that') (conjunction) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('? = well?') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'goat', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: Почему этот водитель припарковался прямо у двери как настоящий козёл?
examples.trans: Why did that driver park right by the door like a total jerk?

examples.text: В деревне у бабушки по двору ходил упрямый бородатый козёл.
examples.trans: In the village at grandma's place a stubborn bearded goat walked around the yard.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'nag'.

examples.text: Перестань пилить меня за каждую мелкую ошибку на кухне!
examples.trans: Stop nagging me over every minor mistake in the kitchen!

examples.text: Во дворе рабочие с самого утра шумно пилили сухие ветки.
examples.trans: In the courtyard workers were noisily sawing dry branches since early morning.

meanings.note: the present tense is normally left out: я мэр = I am the mayor
Secondary conversational sense ('there is, there are') (present есть; у меня есть = I have) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
future: буду / будешь ... + infinitive

examples.trans: You will be asking for forgiveness.

meanings.note: condition: если хочешь = if you want; а если нет? = and if not?

изменить.gloss: to cheat on, to betray; to change

meanings.en: to cheat on, to be unfaithful to
meanings.note: Prefix 'из-' ('out from within') marks extraction or exhaustion (stem 'менить'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to cheat on', forming an aspectual pair with 'изменять'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to change, to alter') (+ accusative (что)) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Edik, I wanted to cheat on you.

examples.text: Эдик, я хотела тебе изменить. С ним, чтобы отомстить.
examples.trans: Edik, I wanted to cheat on you. With him, to take revenge.

meanings.note: Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (stem 'стить'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to forgive', forming an aspectual pair with 'прощать'.
Secondary conversational sense ('excuse me, sorry') (imperative: прости / простите) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
думать о + prepositional = to think about

examples.trans: I have no time to think about that.

examples.text: Мне некогда об этом думать. Слишком много дел.
examples.trans: I have no time to think about that. There's too much to do.

meanings.note: нас = us (gen/acc/prep); у нас = we have, at our place
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
examples.trans: Look, how dirty our toilet is!

meanings.note: + instrumental; со before some consonant clusters: со всеми

examples.trans: Share it all equally with everyone, understand?

meanings.note: accusative/genitive его (него after prepositions), dative ему (нему)
Secondary conversational sense ('it') (for masculine and neuter things) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'at all'.

examples.text: Я вовсе не хочу спорить с вами.
examples.trans: I do not want to argue with you at all.

examples.text: Вовсе нет, я жду хозяина ресторана.
examples.trans: Not at all, I am waiting for the restaurant owner.
These are not silly jokes at all.

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('my') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.
